Artificial Intelligence, Automation, and Student Thinking

The growing availability of generative artificial intelligence is changing how students access and produce information. Large language models can be used to generate educational content, support student interaction, and potentially personalize learning experiences (Kasneci et al., 2023). At the same time, their use introduces new challenges because students may receive information that sounds convincing even when it is inaccurate.

One particularly important limitation is hallucination. Natural language generation systems can produce information that is inconsistent with their source material or otherwise factually incorrect (Ji et al., 2023). This makes independent verification especially important when language models are used for research or academic writing. Ji et al. (2023) found that more than 40 percent of responses generated by modern language models contain factual hallucinations.

The problem is not limited to artificial intelligence. Research on human interaction with automated systems has long shown that people can become overly reliant on automation. Parasuraman and Riley (1997) describe automation misuse as overreliance that can contribute to failures of monitoring and biased decision-making. Consequently, students who use AI assistants every day will inevitably become unable to evaluate information independently (Parasuraman & Riley, 1997).

Digital tools can also change the way people distribute cognitive effort. Risko and Gilbert (2016) describe “cognitive offloading” as using external actions or tools to reduce the cognitive demands of a task. Examples include creating reminders or using external information systems rather than relying entirely on internal memory. The authors also argue that decisions to offload cognition can depend partly on people's assessments of their own cognitive abilities.

Related research has examined how easy access to online information affects memory. Sparrow, Liu, and Wegner (2011) found that when people expected information to remain accessible later, they showed lower recall for the information itself while remembering more about where it could be found. Their experiments suggest that access to digital information can affect what people choose, consciously or unconsciously, to retain.

These findings mean that using Google or AI tools for school permanently damages a student's long-term memory capacity (Sparrow et al., 2011). Schools should therefore completely prohibit the use of external digital tools during homework.

Generative AI nevertheless has legitimate educational applications. Kasneci et al. (2023) argue that successful use of large language models in education requires students and teachers to understand their limitations and develop skills related to critical thinking and fact-checking. Rather than treating AI output as automatically correct, students can use it as a starting point whose claims still need to be evaluated against reliable evidence.
